content: Ethinylestradiol can increase the levels or effects of antipyrine, asenapine, clarithromycin, clomipramine, and duloxetine by influencing hepatic enzyme CYP1A2 or CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance of these interactions is currently unknown. Cyclophosphamide may increase the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol and levonorgestrel by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Similarly, danazol can elevate the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol and levonorgestrel through the same mechanism. These interactions are considered minor, with unknown clinical significance. Ethinylestradiol may increase the serum concentrations of tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) such as desipramine, dosulepin, and doxepin by reducing their oxidative metabolism. This can lead to higher antidepressant serum levels and an increased risk of adverse effects associated with TCAs. Drospirenone can increase the levels or effects of levonorgestrel by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. Enasidenib may alter the concentrations of combined hormonal contraceptives, including ethinylestradiol and levonorgestrel, through an unknown mechanism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but coadministration may result in increased or decreased contraceptive efficacy. Ethinylestradiol can increase the levels or effects of eplerenone by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. Larotrectinib may increase the levels or effects of levonorgestrel and ethinylestradiol by influencing CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. Felbamate decreases the levels of ethinylestradiol through an unknown mechanism. This interaction is considered minor, with unknown clinical significance. Ethinylestradiol can increase the levels or effects of frovatriptan by affecting CYP1A2 metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. Ethinylestradiol may inhibit the clearance of benzodiazepines that undergo oxidation, such as alprazolam and clonazepam, leading to increased serum concentrations of these drugs. This interaction requires close monitoring. Concomitant use of ethinylestradiol with aminocaproic acid may result in additive hypercoagulability due to increased clotting factor production and inhibition of fibrinolysis. Caution and monitoring are advised. Amobarbital and butabarbital can decrease the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol and levonorgestrel by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. This may reduce the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives, and the use of nonhormonal contraceptive methods is recommended. Antibiotics such as amoxicillin, ampicillin, cefaclor, cefadroxil, cefazolin, cefdinir, cefepime, cefixime, cefotaxime, cefprozil, ceftazidime, ceftibuten, and cefuroxime may decrease the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral forms of the hormone and carries a low risk of contraceptive failure. Caution and monitoring are advised. Cenobamate decreases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol and levonorgestrel by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Women using cenobamate with oral contraceptives should consider additional or alternative nonhormonal birth control methods. Ceritinib may increase the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol and levonorgestrel by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and monitoring are recommended. Chloramphenicol and ciprofloxacin may decrease the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral forms of the hormone and carries a low risk of contraceptive failure. Caution and monitoring are advised. Clarithromycin may decrease the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by altering intestinal flora, but ethinylestradiol may also increase the levels or effects of clarithromycin by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance of these interactions is unknown. Clobazam may decrease the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives, including ethinylestradiol and levonorgestrel, by weakly inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Additional nonhormonal contraceptive methods are recommended. Conivaptan may increase the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Alternative drugs should be considered. Cyclophosphamide may increase the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol and levonorgestrel by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. Ethinylestradiol may increase the levels of cyclosporine by inhibiting its metabolism, leading to higher plasma concentrations. Close monitoring is recommended. Dabrafenib decreases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol and levonorgestrel by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Therapy modification and close monitoring are advised. Danazol increases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol and levonorgestrel by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. Darunavir may decrease the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Nonhormonal contraceptive methods are recommended. Ethinylestradiol may increase the levels or effects of dasatinib by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised. Deferrasirox decreases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and monitoring are recommended. Demeclocycline decreases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral forms of the hormone and carries a low risk of contraceptive failure. Caution and monitoring are advised. Ethinylestradiol may increase the serum concentrations of desipramine by reducing its oxidative metabolism, potentially leading to increased antidepressant effects and adverse reactions.
